content.title: About
content.content: Alaska pollock (Theragra chalcogramma) is a marine fish from the cod family that lives in the cold waters of the North Pacific. Raw fillets are light pink, have a mild flavor and a moderately firm texture. Pollock is widely used in the food industry for fillets, fish sticks, patties and canned products.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Pollock is one of the fastest‑growing commercial fish, gaining up to 1.5 kg in a year.
The majority of global pollock production comes from Russia, Canada and the United States.
Raw pollock is rich in omega‑3 fatty acids, which support heart health.
It is often called “white fish” because of its light‑colored flesh after cooking.
In the 2020s, pollock became a popular substitute for more expensive cod in fast‑food menus in the U.S.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Raw pollock provides about 18–20 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3
items.content: EPA and DHA in pollock help lower triglycerides and support brain function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The fish contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Pollock is rich in vitamin B12, niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: It provides selenium, iodine and phosphorus, important for thyroid function and bone health.

items.title: Contaminant risk
items.content: Like many marine species, pollock may contain traces of mercury and other heavy metals; moderate consumption is advised.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Histamine formation
items.content: Improper storage can lead to histamine buildup in raw fish, causing food poisoning.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw pollock is rarely eaten plain but is commonly used for marinated dishes, sushi, and ceviche. Before cooking, rinse the fillet, remove skin and any bones, then slice thinly.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw pollock at 0–2 °C in an airtight container. For longer storage, freeze at ‑18 °C. Before use, check for a strong ammonia‑like odor; discard if the smell is off.
